text.p: German chemicals and drugs group Hoechst AG said on Tuesday it was transferring all rights for the controversial abortion pill RU-486 to a former manager and would now cease production of the drug completely.

Hoechst, which has suffered considerable damage to its image through its association with the pill, which allows a women to terminate a pregnancy without surgery, said the transfer fitted its strategy of refocusing its pharmaceutical operations in its global drugs unit, Hoechst Marion Roussel.
"We have divorced ourselves completely from RU-486 as part of the business of tidying-up and giving new strategic direction to HMR," a Hoechst spokesman said.
The pill was acclaimed by women's rights groups but became the target of fierce protests from anti-abortionists.

The patent rights for the drug, the medical term for which is mifepristine, had been transferred with immediate effect to Edouard Sakiz, a developer of the product, who recently retired as supervisory board chairman at Hoechst's French subsidiary Roussel Uclaf, at no cost to Sakiz.

Hoechst, the world's largest chemicals group, had acquired a stake in the French drugs group Roussel Uclaf years ago and has since integrated that stake and its U.S. acquisition Marion Merrell Dow into Hoechst Marion Roussel.
Hoechst, which has seen only six million marks ($3.5 million) of sales in the drug, took over the rights for RU-486.
In the United States, Hoechst had already transferred the rights for the drug to the non-profit organisation The Population Council at the request of the U.S. government.

But the transfer failed to still U.S. anti-abortion capaigners, who just a few days ago launched a newspaper advertising campaign urging consumers to boycott HMR's allergy drug Allegra, a new product available only in the United States.
In Europe, the anti-abortion pill is currently only marketed in France, Britain and Sweden.

In Germany too, the pill has stirred controversy. Some politicians have called for Hoechst to launch the pill on the German market to make abortion easier for women despite protests against the drug by by pro-life groups.
Hoechst has so far followed a policy of introducing the drug only if a nation's government has expressly asked it to launch the drug.
"At the moment we have such an application from Switzerland, but not from Germany," a spokeswoman for Roussel Uclaf in Paris said in answer to Reuters enquiries.
She added that Sakiz would follow the same launch policy as had been adopted by Hoechst.
As a result of the transfer, Roussel Uclaf will cease manufacturing, marketing and distribution of the drug.
